headline: Half of Dementia Cases May Be Preventable, New Study Shows
meta_description: Lund University research reveals nearly half of dementia cases link to modifiable risk factors like smoking and high blood pressure.
summary_short: A four-year brain study from Lund University found that smoking, high blood pressure, and heart disease are strongly linked to dementia—and changing these habits could h…
body:
Researchers at Lund University have uncovered hopeful news in the fight against dementia: nearly half of all cases may be connected to risk factors people can actually change. A four-year study of almost 500 cognitively healthy participants, with an average age of 65, tracked how lifestyle choices and health conditions affected brain changes associated with Alzheimer's disease and vascular dementia. The findings reveal that smoking, high blood pressure, cardiovascular disease, and high blood lipids were all linked to damage in the brain's blood vessels and faster accumulation of white matter changes—the nerve fibers often harmed in vascular dementia.

What makes this research particularly significant is that it examined how different risk factors affect the two most common types of dementia separately, rather than treating dementia as one condition. Senior lecturer Sebastian Palmqvist from Skåne University Hospital explained that previous research often overlooked these distinctions, leaving gaps in our understanding of which lifestyle changes matter most for which type of disease. The study also found tentative connections between diabetes and increased buildup of amyloid-β protein, and between lower BMI and faster tau accumulation—though these findings require further investigation.

Perhaps most encouraging is that many people develop multiple forms of brain damage simultaneously. This means that adopting healthier habits addresses several harmful processes at once. By focusing on vascular and metabolic health—controlling blood pressure, quitting smoking, managing cholesterol, and maintaining physical activity—people may be able to reduce the combined effects of different brain changes. While age, gender, and genetics remain uncontrollable factors, the research suggests that the choices we make today could meaningfully delay dementia's appearance tomorrow.
quick_facts: Lund University tracked 500 participants over four years
Smoking, high blood pressure, and heart disease linked to brain damage
Nearly half of dementia cases tied to changeable risk factors
Study examined Alzheimer's and vascular dementia separately
